name: Hassan Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a usual day on site like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and build timber stud partitions on building sites, including the openings around pipes and ducts. My trade certificate and years on crews make me dependable, though I am not the fastest hand. I earn a good rate and still show apprentices how to find a straight line on a crooked slab. I have never used an AI tool; my partner and I have grown children, more than six months of expenses saved and a hope of retiring at sixty-seven in 2035 if our income allows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the young hands that a faster board order is fine, but a fire-rated wall still needs its gaps sealed. An AI materials list cannot seal a hole around a pipe in a building wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the good wage to continue. With more than six months saved and plenty of similar nearby jobs, my partner and I have room to check retirement figures without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep framing partitions, checking the pipe openings and showing the apprentice how to fit each seal. I would ask my partner to compare our expected age-sixty-seven income with ordinary household costs before any retirement decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work here. I am content to let the office use a computer while I do the fitting correctly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you show the apprentice at a pipe opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fire-stopping label and the actual gap, then how to fit the approved seal. A gap hidden by a board can fail a whole wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the budget review mean retiring sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Sixty-seven in 2035 is already the age I hope for, and we will keep earning until we know the figures cover our life.

say: I would **keep** fitting fire-rated partitions and teach careful sealing.
I would **tell** the crew office lists cannot substitute for a site gap check.
think: Our **good** wage, strong savings and many nearby jobs make this stable.
The **age-sixty-seven** budget is information, not an exit notice.
do: **Keep** framing partitions and checking approved fire seals around pipes.
**Review** age-sixty-seven household income against costs with partner.
feel: **Calm** about paid site work and the existing retirement plan.
S0.quote: An AI materials list cannot seal a hole around a pipe in a building wall.
fieldNote: **Hassan** never uses AI and values practical apprenticeships and fire-rated partition checks.
**High** wages, strong savings and many nearby builders make the plateau financially secure.

steps.text: Keep fitting and checking fire-rated site partitions
Check original age-sixty-seven retirement budget before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster AI building plan cannot make a missing paid fire-seal check safe. I would stand beside the apprentice while we inspect the openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my basic wage would probably hold, yet a tighter schedule might reduce my overtime. Our savings make that manageable, though I do not like the idea of a missing paid inspection being called efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the partition shifts and record the time it takes to check service openings on two jobs. If the builder cuts those hours, I would ask for written terms and compare posted local partition roles only where wages cover our bills and safety time is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible loss of my own paid hours, with enough reserve to negotiate. I still do not plan to learn an AI tool I will not use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove the check needs that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark each service opening and the approved seal on the site sheet, then show the builder the hours on two jobs. The record would be physical and dated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another builder quickly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would first see whether a posted nearby role states the wage and paid inspection time. We have savings, so I can refuse a rushed offer.

say: I would **insist** on paid fire-seal checks when AI speeds planning.
I would **show** the builder actual site hours from two partition jobs.
think: My **overtime** could shrink even if the basic rate stays.
**Strong** savings let me refuse a local role without paid safety time.
do: **Record** fire-seal inspection hours on two building jobs.
**Keep** paid partition shifts while seeking written hour terms.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local partition role with adequate pay and paid safety checks.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible own-hour loss, with a strong reserve.
S1.quote: A faster AI building plan cannot make a missing paid fire-seal check safe.
fieldNote: He **resists** AI use but is willing to document site work and negotiate paid checks.
A **possible** overtime reduction affects his income, despite strong savings and many alternative builders.

steps.text: Keep paid partition work while documenting checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives in 2028 when I am sixty, but hands-on robots follow around 2031 when I am sixty-three. Four possible wage years stand between those robots and my planned retirement at sixty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose paid partition work when machines frame standard walls. We have a long cash cushion and many nearby builders, but I would rather earn my way to the age we planned than spend savings early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep framing and ask for a written human fire-seal inspection rule before any robot-built wall is closed. If paid hours fell after 2031, I would apply to posted local repair-partition jobs only if wages cover our household and I have safe access and stop-work authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the four-year gap, though I have options. I would not retire at sixty-three unless verified income covered all the later bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which robot-built wall would you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot could close a partition in 2031 before anyone sees the fire seal around the pipe. I would require the board opened and the seal inspected before sign-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your savings let you leave at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have not made that calculation. More than six months saved is useful, but it is not four years of wages plus a whole retirement.

say: **Thinking** AI changes plans in 2028; robots may frame walls around 2031.
I would **demand** a human fire-seal check before robot-built walls close.
think: **Four** wage years could be at risk before my original retirement target.
A **posted** local repair role needs bill-covering pay and safe stop-work authority.
do: **Keep** paid partition work while demanding written robot-wall fire checks.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local repair role with adequate wage and safe stop-work authority.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible four-year earnings gap, with choices.
S2.quote: A robot could close a partition in 2031 before anyone sees the fire seal around the pipe.
fieldNote: He **keeps** thinking automation in 2028 separate from physical robots around 2031.
**Strong** savings do not justify an unverified early exit; any application needs a real safe local role with adequate pay.

steps.text: Keep paid framing while requiring human robot-wall fire checks
Apply after cuts to posted local repair job with adequate pay and stop-work authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am sixty-three, and site robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. That puts the physical machines one year before my hoped-for retirement at sixty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A 2034 robot may take the last year of partition wages I meant to earn before 2035. I would check expected household income first and still want a real paid role if the numbers do not cover us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the partition shifts and review the age-sixty-seven budget with my partner. If robots cut hours in 2034, I would apply to a posted nearby fire-stopping job only if the wage covers bills and safe access and stop-work authority are written; I would leave at the original target only if income permits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible final-year wage loss, but less pressed than in the fast case. I can check figures and local openings before deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a course help you get a fire-stopping job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a suitable local vacancy were posted, the course fully funded and its training days paid. I would not enroll just to collect paper at sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the household calculation pass?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Expected ongoing income must cover ordinary bills and repairs without using the cash reserve up quickly. We will check that before I give notice.

say: **Robots** around 2034 could affect the final year before my planned retirement.
I would **keep** paid site work until verified income covers the household.
think: **One** lost wage year is possible, though savings may bridge it.
A **real** local fire-stopping job requires adequate pay and written safety authority.
do: **Review** age-sixty-seven household income and ongoing costs.
**Keep** paid partition shifts while robot work is assessed.
**Apply** after 2034 cuts to posted local fire-stopping role with adequate pay and safe authority.
feel: **Anxious** about possible final-year income loss, with time to check.
S3.quote: A 2034 robot may take the last year of partition wages I meant to earn before 2035.
fieldNote: His 2035 **target** is one year after the 2034 physical robot date and remains conditional on income.
A **course** question is only information; any actual job move needs a posted local adequate safe role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am sixty-eight, with capable site robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. A 2039 partition robot cannot dismiss me from a site I left in 2035, if our retirement sums hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would rather be teaching a grandchild how to mark timber than claiming I will still be on a site at seventy-one. If the budget fails, I may work longer, but only at a safe paid job with a real local opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep present paid partition shifts while my partner and I verify retirement income. If it covers the bills, I would retire at the original 2035 target; if not, I would apply only to posted nearby repair work at a household-covering wage with safe access and the right to stop a bad wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until the figures are done, but calm about the distant robot if we can afford to leave. The younger workers still deserve proper hand skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep an apprentice after retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might show a family member some hand work, but I would not claim a paid teaching job without a posted place and wage. I prefer to teach on a real wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the retirement budget falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep earning on a posted safe local repair job that covers our bills. A prediction about robots does not decide the household budget.

I would **keep** working only if verified household income falls short.
think: I do **not** assume a paid site role at seventy-one.
A **later** repair job needs a posted local opening, adequate pay and safe authority.
do: **Keep** present paid partition work while verifying retirement figures.
**Retire** at original 2035 target only if income covers ongoing bills.
**Apply** if still working to posted local safe repair role at household-covering wage.
feel: **Uneasy** until the budget is checked, otherwise calm about distant robots.
S4.quote: A 2039 partition robot cannot dismiss me from a site I left in 2035, if our retirement sums hold.
fieldNote: His **original** age-sixty-seven retirement is income-conditional, not an early machine-driven exit.
**Any** work after 2035 is conditional on a budget shortfall and a posted safe local job with adequate wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because 2031 robots could cost four partition wages before my planned exit. Written fire-seal checks and a posted local repair role with adequate pay and safe authority would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who inspects the pipe opening before a robot closes a wall. A fast machine and a good wage are no comfort if the fire seal is hidden. I will take a slower carpenter with a visible fire seal over a fast robot that closes the wall first.

headlineQuote: I will take a slower carpenter with a visible fire seal over a fast robot that closes the wall first.
portrait: **Hassan** is a fifty-eight-year-old trade-certified construction worker who frames fire-rated timber partitions.
He **earns** higher pay, has over six months saved, a partner, grown children and many local jobs.
He **never** uses AI, values apprenticeships and hopes to retire at sixty-seven in 2035 if income covers bills.
**Fast** robots threaten pre-retirement wages; later work is conditional on the verified budget and safe posted local roles.
biggestWorry: The **fast** 2031 robot arrival could cut partition wages four years before his original retirement target.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** human fire-seal checks and a posted nearby repair role with adequate pay and safe stop-work authority would help.
